name: Lorazepam
meta: Psychotropic substance under the NDPS Act, 1985 and Schedule H/H1 of the Drugs &
sections: Nearly white powder, poorly soluble in water.
A 3-hydroxy benzodiazepine; on the WHO List of Essential Medicines and among the most prescribed anxiolytics. First approval/introduction: Patented 1963; introduced 1977 (Wyeth Pharmaceuticals).

Binds the benzodiazepine site of GABA-A receptors, increasing chloride-channel opening frequency and producing anxiolytic, sedative, anticonvulsant and muscle-relaxant effects. Receptor / target profile: Increases chloride-channel opening frequency at GABA-A receptors; high receptor affinity gives pronounced anxiolytic, sedative and amnesic effects.
Summary: Bioavailability ~90%; Tmax ~2 h. ~85% protein bound. Directly glucuronidated (no active metabolites; suitable in hepatic impairment/elderly with care). Half-life 10–20 h.
Short-term relief of anxiety and anxiety associated with depressive symptoms
Anxiety: 1–4 mg/day in divided doses (range up to 10 mg/day)
Insomnia due to anxiety: 1–2 mg at bedtime
Dose to be individualised by the treating physician according to clinical response and tolerability.
Use with caution; accumulation of glucuronide.
Preferred benzodiazepine in hepatic impairment (no oxidative metabolism) but use with caution; avoid in encephalopathy.
Not recommended for oral anxiety use <12 years.
Dependence and withdrawal – limit duration; taper
Valproate and probenecid raise lorazepam levels
Drowsiness, confusion, ataxia, hypotension, respiratory depression, coma. Supportive care; flumazenil with caution.
Alldredge et al., NEJM 2001 – pre-hospital IV lorazepam effective in status epilepticus.
Short-term efficacy in anxiety established in early placebo-controlled trials; long-term use limited by dependence.
Do not drive or operate machinery
Store below 30°C in a dry place, protected from light and moisture. Keep out of the reach of children. Do not use after the expiry date.
